opening.headline: Understand what comes and goes when assigning tasks to different agents, and learn how to judge the conditions under which multi-agent use is beneficial.
body: It may seem that more agents will make things faster, but in reality, it can actually slow things down and increase costs. Conversely, if you leave everything to a single agent, the context will be overloaded and forward instructions will be pushed out. What is important is the standard for deciding whether to share or not.

In this lesson, we compare how handoffs and agent-as-tools handle ownership of answers differently, explore the benefits of subagents, and the architecture of multi-agent research systems. Next, we explain cases where context separation is the reason and cases where multi-agent is not beneficial, and summarize the conditions for benefit in a checklist.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain handoff, subagent, and multi-agent research structures
Can determine conditions under which multi-agent is beneficial

screens.title: An agent's context explodes.
screens.lead: First, read the results of entrusting a large investigation to one agent. As you read, think about what the bottleneck is.

visual.alt: A scene where an agent chat window is filled with search results and the front part is cut off.
labels: Instructions: Survey the boards of directors of 20 competitors.
Re-investigating companies we have already researched

paragraphs: One team asked an agent to “research the boards of directors of 20 of our competitors.” Agents searched for companies one by one and read each page, with search results and file contents stacked into one conversation. At some point, the bar representing the context fills up.

As the instructions and memos from the front were pushed aside, the back office began to reinvestigate the companies it had already investigated. It took a long time because I processed them one by one in order. It may seem like things will get better if you add more agents, but the more agents there are, the slower it gets and the cost increases.

This is the underlying principle of the context window. Model calls are stateless, so they have to resend the entire history so far each turn, and there is a limit to the amount of tokens that can be handled at one time. Even if it is within the limit, research has shown that if the input is long, the degree to which information placed in the center is utilized decreases (Liu et al., 2023, TACL 2024). A typical way to circumvent this limitation is to split the work so that each agent starts in a new context with only the information it needs.

This is the question this class addresses. What goes back and forth when tasks are divided, and who is responsible for the final answer? And what are the conditions under which it is beneficial to divide agents?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If four agents are responsible for investigating 20 companies, should each agent hand over the entire investigation to each other, or just a summary?

screens.outro: Let me first think about whether you have had a similar experience.

ext.title: Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (TACL, 2024)

screens.title: Think of similar scenes
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think in your head first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever had an experience where the model forgot the conditions mentioned earlier during a long conversation?
items.answer: As the conversation gets longer, the context window fills up, crowding out the beginning or getting buried in the middle. It's not that the model has forgotten, it's that it can no longer effectively see the information it needs. Solving this problem structurally is the starting point of this class.

items.prompt: Even in human teams, when has there ever been a time when instead of one person doing everything, you hand it over to an expert?
items.answer: When a task exceeds one person's time and attention, or requires specialized knowledge, it is passed on to a professional. The same goes for agents. The key to design is deciding who to hand over work to and who is responsible for the results.

items.prompt: Have you ever had an experience where you missed information while flipping through it and had to explain it again?
items.answer: Delegation comes at a cost. If the explanation is poor, work will be duplicated or gaps will be created. So your delegation design needs to be clear about what to hand over and what to get back.

screens.outro: First, let's look at the differences between two methods of delegation: handoff and agent-as-tool.

screens.title: Handoffs and agent-as-tools: who owns the answers
screens.lead: Select the "Handoff" and "Agent-as-Tool" buttons alternately to compare how the two delegation methods handle ownership of the answer differently.

states.label: handoff
states.body: Control is handed over to a specialized agent to take charge of the next response for the quarter. For example, a triage agent passes a refund inquiry to a refund agent, who then takes over the conversation with the user. Handoff in the OpenAI Agents SDK appears to be a tool for LLM. The handoff to the Refund Agent results in a tool name of `transfer_to_refund_agent`. `handoff_description` can be short and specific so the model knows when to pick this handoff, and the input filter can filter out the conversation history that the next agent receives.

states.label: agent-as-tool
states.body: The main agent is responsible for the final answer and calls on experts with limited functions such as summarization or classification. The outer workflow remains one and expert calls are nested inside it. It is suitable when administrators need to synthesize the results of multiple experts and provide answers to users. The expert works like a tool, and the person who communicates with the user is the main agent until the end. The selection criteria is simple. It's a handoff when an expert needs to take over the conversation, or an agent-as-tool when a manager needs to synthesize it. Additionally, if possible, start with one agent and only add experts when it significantly improves ability isolation, policy isolation, prompt clarity, and trace readability.

screens.outro: Now that we've compared delegation approaches, let's look at subagents and context separation.

screens.title: Separate subagent and context
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term to see an explanation. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: Sub-agents are separate agent instances launched by the main agent, each responsible for narrow sub-tasks. The biggest advantage is Context separation. Sub-agents start their own conversation, handle intermediate tool calls and results internally, and only return the final message to the main agent. Even if they read dozens of files, they only accumulate summaries in the main agent's conversation. The second advantage is Parallelization. Independent sub-tasks run concurrently, and the overall time is limited only by the slowest task—such as performing style checks, security scans, and test coverage simultaneously. The third advantage is specialized instruction, allowing each sub-agent to have its own appropriate system prompt. The fourth advantage is tool limitations, reducing unintended modification risks by providing only read-only tools. The definition method involves the code's agents parameters, Markdown files under the .claude/agents/ directory, and pre-provided generic sub-agents are available by default. However, short tasks and steps that depend on each other should be left to the main agent, and coordination is required among agents that modify the same file.

terms.tip: The design is to keep the intermediate processes of the sub-agent within it and return only the final message to the main agent. The main dialogue becomes lighter.
It is the simultaneous execution of independent subtasks. The overall time is the time of the slowest task, not the sum of each time.
Each subagent has its own system prompt to contain expertise and constraints.
This setting narrows the tools a subagent can use. If you give it a read-only tool, you can analyze it but not edit it.
This is a way to define subagents directly in SDK code. Include a description, prompt, and tool to use.

screens.outro: Let’s look at an example that maximizes this benefit: a multi-agent research system.

screens.title: Multi-agent research system structure diagram
screens.lead: Select the number marker in the picture to see a detailed explanation. Check the markers one by one.

visual.alt: A structure diagram in which the lead agent divides work among several sub-agents and receives compressed results.

markers.label: lead agent
markers.title: Analyze inquiries and develop strategies
markers.body: The lead agent analyzes user queries, develops strategies, and creates sub-agents. Because research is an open problem whose steps cannot be known in advance, a fixed path cannot be set, and the model must change direction based on discoveries. The structure is orchestrator-worker.

markers.label: subagent
markers.title: Explore different aspects simultaneously
markers.body: Subagents explore different aspects simultaneously. It works as an intelligent filter that filters information through repeated searches, condensing only the most important content and returning it to leads.

markers.label: memory
markers.title: Save the plan to memory
markers.body: Reed stores the plan in memory because the context is truncated when it exceeds the limit. Even if the context is cut off, the plan can be reread and continued.

markers.label: Compressed results
markers.title: Only a summary is returned to Reed.
markers.body: Subagent's intermediate search results and file contents do not go to the lead. Since all you get back is a condensed result, the lead's context is kept light enough to cover the synthesis step.

markers.label: Benefits and Costs
markers.title: Benefits from breadth-first queries: tokens increase significantly
markers.body: In an internal evaluation of the document, lead and sub-agent configurations were 90.2% higher than single agents. The benefit is large for breadth-first queries. The price is also high. Agents spend about 4 times as many tokens as chat, and multi-agent uses about 15 times as many tokens. Economics only make sense when the value of the work is high enough.

screens.outro: Operating this structure requires a delegated design and management approach.

screens.title: Delegated design and managed multi-agent
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how to design delegation well and how multi-agent operates in a managed environment.

tabs.label: teaches delegation
tabs.body: Lead agents must learn how to delegate to sub-agents. Each subagent is given a goal, output format, instructions on what tools and sources to use, and the boundaries of the task. If the explanation is poor, work will be duplicated or gaps will be created. The same search may be repeated by both agents, or some parts will remain that no one is responsible for, and so on.

tabs.label: Effort Distribution Rules
tabs.body: Include in the prompt rules to allocate effort based on the complexity of the query. A simple fact check requires just a few tool calls per agent. Comparisons are performed by several sub-agents, and complex studies are performed by multiple sub-agents who share responsibilities. Without rules, you end up spending too much resources on even simple questions.

tabs.label: Reduce the passing game
tabs.body: If you have the sub-agent leave the results in the file system, you can reduce the transmission game where information is corrupted as it passes through the leads. Tokens are also saved because you only need to return a file reference to the lead.

tabs.label: Managed multi-agent
tabs.body: There are three approaches to Managed Multi-Agents: These include delegating to sub-agents, dynamic workflows where agents write programs that run multiple agents, and consulting an advisor model. All agents share the same sandbox and filesystem, but each runs on an isolated session thread, or its own conversation log.

tabs.label: cost management
tabs.body: All tokens spent by an agent are aggregated, so they are capped by the session budget. It also lets you know when to write a workflow at the system prompt, preventing unnecessary expansion.

screens.outro: Now that you have learned the concept, let's explain it with an example.

screens.title: Commentary 1: Cases where context separation is the reason
screens.lead: The instructor explains a case where the reason for having a subagent is context separation, not speed. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: request
steps.body: This is a request to check security vulnerabilities in large repositories and produce a summary report. There are hundreds of files to read, and the final output is a short report. The structure involves a lot of reading and little writing. These types of requests are easy to entrust to a single agent, but they have the highest context cost.

steps.title: Single agent problem
steps.body: When a single agent does this, the contents of hundreds of files are piled into one conversation. When writing a report, the evidence is pushed aside, and time and money are spent re-checking files that have already been viewed. This problem arises structurally, regardless of the model's performance.

steps.title: Subagent configuration
steps.body: The security scanner subagent reads the file and returns only the suspect list as the final message. This subagent is given read-only tools. Although it can analyze, it cannot fix the code, reducing the risk of unintentional modifications.

steps.title: Main agent's context
steps.body: Only the summarized list is stacked in the main agent's context. The synthesis step is light, and all the evidence needed to write the report remains in context. Since the contents of files read by subagents do not remain in the main conversation, many more follow-up questions can be asked in the same context.

steps.title: judgment
steps.body: In this case, the reason for having subagents is context separation, not speed. You can gain speed by doing the same thing in parallel, but the key gain comes from keeping the main conversation clean. So if report quality is an issue, look at context first, not speed.

screens.outro: Next, let's look at a case where multi-agent is not beneficial.

screens.title: Commentary 2: When multi-agent is not beneficial
screens.lead: Switch between the “Divided” and “Undivided” buttons to compare how the same task works differently. Compare the two states and see which one handles dependencies better.

states.label: When divided into multi-agent
states.body: There is a task of modifying the same configuration file step by step. The result of the previous step is the input to the next step. If you divide this in parallel, the agents will crash while editing the same file at the same time, and coordination costs will increase as they have to coordinate each other's changes. Anthropic's article introducing the multi-agent research system explains that domains where all agents must share the same context or where there is a lot of dependency between agents do not fit well with multi-agent. Cognition's Walden Yan also argued in his 2025 article "Don't Build Multi-Agents" that sub-agents that do not sufficiently share context are likely to act based on misaligned assumptions. Both are design experiences based on actual cases and are not rules proven through experimentation. Additionally, multi-agent can spend up to 15 times as many tokens as chat, so it is not economical if the value of the work is low. For example, if three agents change different items in their configuration files simultaneously, later changes may overwrite earlier changes. To prevent this, a separate coordination device is needed to set the order, and that device becomes more complicated than the task.

states.label: When placed on one main agent
states.body: Tasks where steps depend on each other and keep changing the same state are better handled sequentially by a single main agent. The results of the previous step are inherited, no conflicts occur, and fewer tokens are used. As a rule, short tasks and dependent steps should be placed in the main agent. Experts add isolation only when the benefits are clear. In this case, you don't gain speed, but you gain accuracy and simplicity. In tasks with strong dependencies, these two are more important. In this configuration, the tool only gives you what you need and leaves intermediate results in a file so you can continue even if the work is interrupted.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will organize the beneficial conditions into a checklist.

ext.title: Anthropic, How we built our multi-agent research system (2025)

screens.title: Commentary 3: Checklist of beneficial conditions
screens.lead: When you select each question, an explanation will unfold. Apply it one by one to each case of investigating a competitor’s board of directors. See the last item for your final judgment.

items.prompt: Are there multiple subtasks that can be broken down independently?
items.answer: If it is breadth-first research, then yes. Since the 20 companies are independent of each other, they can be divided by company or by group of companies. Parallelization benefits when subtasks do not have to wait for each other's results. It is up to the lead to combine the results.

items.prompt: Is it possible to compress and return the results of each subtask?
items.answer: If the main agent only needs a summary, then yes. Intermediate search results can be placed inside a subagent, since all you need to get back are board member names and titles. The benefits of context separation are diminished if you have to hand over all the details.

items.prompt: Does the value of the work cover the increased token cost?
items.answer: If you do deep research, yes. Multi-agent consumes approximately 15 times as many tokens as a chat, making it unsuitable for simple confirmations that can be completed in a matter of minutes. First, consider whether the work is worthwhile enough to justify the cost. If the value is low, a single agent is better.

items.prompt: Don't subtasks keep changing the same state?
items.answer: Yes, if you focus on reading. Since most of the research involves reading, there is no conflict. Editing the same file requires coordination and is therefore not suitable.

items.prompt: What if all four of your questions are answered?
items.answer: Consider multi-agent. If not one, use a single agent or workflow. If possible, start with one agent, and add experts only when it significantly improves ability isolation, policy isolation, prompt clarity, and trace readability. This checklist is a short set of questions you can ask each time before sharing.

screens.outro: Now, let's organize the concepts of this lesson into a map.

screens.title: Concept map revisited
screens.lead: Select and expand each concept to see how it connects to the problem in the first scene.

items.title: handoff
items.body: Hand over ownership of the conversation to an expert. The expert is responsible for responding after submission.

items.title: subagent
items.body: It works in its own context and only returns the final message. Reduces the problem of the main conversation popping up.

items.title: research system
items.body: This is a structure where the lead develops a strategy and the parallel sub-agent returns the compressed results. There are significant benefits from breadth-first research. Since only compressed results are returned, the lead's context is also protected.

items.title: Context separation
items.body: This is the biggest reason to keep the main agent's conversation light. Context protection is often prioritized over speed.

items.title: Managed multi-agent
items.body: Operates with isolated session threads and session budgets. All tokens used by agents are added up.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the judgment criteria one more time.

screens.title: Check before splitting agents
screens.lead: The content of this lesson is organized into design judgments. Read it slowly.

paragraphs: Before splitting agents, first check if one agent is enough. It checks whether the context is full, whether there are independent subtasks, whether the results can be returned compressed, and whether the token cost is worth it.

If you decide to divide, decide how to delegate. Use Handoff when an expert needs to take over the conversation, Agent-as-Tool when a manager needs to synthesize, and Subagent when you want to hide the middleman and only summarize. Give subagents clear goals, output formats, tools, and boundaries, and cap them with a session budget.
Check the designed configuration through evaluation. Only when comparing the results of a single agent and the results of a split configuration with the same inputs can the split gains be trusted.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: It doesn't get better with more agents. Only independent, high-value operations will benefit, and token costs will increase significantly.

glossary.def: This is a delegation method that passes ownership of the next response to a professional agent.
This is an agent instance in a separate context launched by the main agent.
The design is to place the intermediate process within a sub-agent and return only the final message to the main agent.
Event flow of conversation history isolated per agent in a managed environment.
This is a coordinator who analyzes queries, creates strategies, and distributes work to sub-agents.

misconceptions.fact: There are gains only in independent, high-value work. Token costs can increase to approximately 15 times that of chat, and dependent operations only increase coordination costs.

misconceptions.myth: Subagents are used only for speed.
misconceptions.fact: Context separation and tool limitations are also big reasons. It keeps the main conversation light and prevents unintentional modifications with read-only tools.

misconceptions.myth: Handoff and agent-as-tool are the same thing.
misconceptions.fact: A handoff transfers ownership of the conversation to an expert, while an agent-as-tool keeps the manager responsible for the final answer.

closing.lead: The key contents of this class are summarized as follows.
points: Handoff transfers control, and agent-as-tool leaves the manager responsible for the final answer.
Sub-agents work in their own context and only return a summary, sparing the main agent's context.
The research system is an orchestrator-worker structure consisting of a lead agent and parallel sub-agents.
Multi-agent benefits from breadth-first independent operations, and tokens can grow to about 15x the chat.
Dependent short tasks are left on the main agent, and experts are added only when the benefit of isolation is clear.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for you to think about for yourself. We will not submit or grade your answers, so feel free to think about them.
closing.reflection: What tasks in my job would fill up the context if I left it to one agent? If you divide it up, are the subtasks independent of each other?
